headline: Double Creek Fluke Slide Toward the Inlet — Weakfish Spikes Working the Tices Shoal Flats
subhead: Warm bay water has pushed the fluke bite toward Barnegat Inlet while bunker start showing near the rocks — the first real clue fall stripers aren't far behind.
body_markdown:
Forty Augusts ago my uncle Nick used to say the bay gets "tired" this time of year — water sits too long under a high sun, the channels hold heat down deep, and every fish with a choice starts looking for a way out toward the inlet. He wasn't wrong then and he's not wrong now. That's exactly the pattern setting up on Barnegat Bay this week, and it's the same one we flagged a few days back — expect fluke fishing to stay modest until the nights cool enough to break up that warm layer sitting on the bottom. Well, the nights haven't cooled much yet, and the fluke have voted with their fins.

Through the back half of August the bay held onto its summer heat stubbornly, and that's pushed fluke out of the mid-bay flats and into the better-oxygenated water near Barnegat Inlet, Double Creek Channel, and the deeper cuts off Barnegat Light. Anybody working the shallow sod banks up around Toms River or the flats off Good Luck Point has been finding mostly shorts and the occasional keeper, but the real keeper activity has shifted down toward the inlet structure where the tide runs harder and the water stays cooler on the bottom. Boats working the edges of Double Creek Channel on the last two hours of the outgoing tide have had the better of it, dragging 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail right along the channel drop where the mud gives way to shell. Fish to four and five pounds have come from there, but it's not a bucket bite — you're working for every keeper, and the shorts still outnumber them three or four to one on most drifts.

Weakfish have been the pleasant surprise. The classic May pattern up at the sedge banks doesn't repeat itself in September the same way, but there's a real spike of weakfish working the grass edges around Tices Shoal and the flats south of there on the last of the incoming tide, particularly in that hour before the top when the current still has some push to it. These aren't the springtime spawners — smaller, feistier fish in the 14 to 18-inch range, but they're eating well on small pink or chartreuse Gulp shrimp fished on a light jighead, worked slow just off bottom in three to five feet of water. Anybody who remembers to slow down and let the bait sit a beat longer than instinct tells them has been doing better than the guys ripping it through.

Snapper blues are everywhere right now, which is normal for this stretch of summer into early fall — small blues chasing peanut bunker and spearing up in the skinny water off Island Beach and around the Oyster Creek outflow, where that warm discharge water still draws bait even this late in the season. Kids with a bobber and a strip of bunker under a dock at Forked River or up around Cedar Creek are having no trouble filling an afternoon. The bigger cocktail blues, three and four pounds, have been mixing into the bunker pods that are just starting to show near the inlet rocks — and that bunker buildup is the thing to watch closest over the next two weeks. It's early, but it's there, and that's usually the first domino before the fall striper run gets moving in this part of the bay. Nothing dramatic yet on stripers themselves — a few schoolies have shown around the inlet jetties on the last of the ebb, mostly incidental fish mixed in with the blues, nothing worth planning a trip around.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around the usual haunts — blowfish thick around the docks and bulkheads in Forked River and Waretown on clam bits fished on a high-low rig, kingfish working the surf troughs at Island Beach State Park on bloodworm or Fishbites during the calmer tide stages. Nothing exceptional, but steady if you've got the patience for small baits and light line.

Looking at the water and the calendar, this holding pattern probably continues through the first few days of September. Nights haven't dropped enough yet to flip that thermal layering in the bay, and until they do, fluke will keep favoring the inlet-adjacent structure over the open flats. If you've only got one day this weekend, fish the last two hours of the outgoing on Double Creek Channel for fluke, then slide over to Tices Shoal for the last hour of the incoming for weakfish and snapper blues — that covers both tide stages without burning the whole day running around. Keep an eye on the bunker schools near the inlet rocks; if they thicken up over the next week or two the way they usually do heading into September, that's your signal the first real fall striper push into the bay is close. Until then, this is patient-man fishing — work the edges, mind the tide, and don't expect a bucket, but there's enough moving to make the trip worthwhile.
